title: Your Perception Of Time Is, In Fact, Warped | NOEMA
gist: A widespread post-2020 sense that time is 'speeding up' is explained by new time-perception science: the brain has no internal clock and instead infers duration from the volume of sensory/informational change it processes and from how many memories a period leaves behind — meaning smartphone/social-media saturation compresses lived time while simultaneously erasing the memories needed to make that time feel full in retrospect.

themes.theme: The end of the 'internal clock' model

insights.claim: Time perception researchers have largely abandoned the long-standing 'internal clock model' (the idea that the brain has a dedicated oscillator counting time units like a man-made clock) because decades of study never found evidence of such a mechanism.
insights.speaker: Mike Mariani
insights.so_what: Reframes any product or wellness claim built on 'resetting your internal clock' as scientifically outdated; useful context for evaluating digital-wellbeing and neurotech marketing claims.
insights.quote: You have some oscillator ticking away at some frequency, and then counting the time units, much like clocks work.
insights.locator: The Internal Clock Fallacy, quoting Dean Buonomano

insights.claim: A 2022 University of Sussex study (Roseboom et al.) found that subjective time perception correlates with the amount of change/activity the brain's visual processing detects in a stimulus, leading to the theory that humans tell time via 'the accumulation of salient changes in the perceptual processing hierarchy' rather than any fixed internal duration sense.
insights.speaker: Mike Mariani
insights.so_what: Provides a testable mechanistic model (perceptual 'stuff-counting') that could underlie product design decisions in social media, gaming, and streaming — an app that maximizes content-switching per minute could be quantifiably altering measured user time-perception, which regulators or app-store policy could someday target.
insights.quote: the brain just ‘counts’ how much ‘stuff’ has happened, which is very intuitive
insights.locator: The Internal Clock Fallacy, Roseboom co-author quote

insights.claim: Because digital media floods the brain with far more visual/informational 'stuff' per minute than in-person life did 10-20 years ago, the perceptual-change-counting mechanism causes people to register time as passing faster while actually engaged with devices.
insights.speaker: James Hyman
insights.so_what: Gives a mechanistic causal story linking screen-time intensity to the 'time is speeding up' zeitgeist — relevant to any company or policymaker assessing the psychological cost side of the attention economy.
insights.quote: We’re constantly moving onto the next thing. And the more things that we experience that cause us to move forward, well, if our brains are only able to tell time by counting things, then we’re jamming lots more things in there.
insights.locator: The Internal Clock Fallacy, James Hyman quote

themes.theme: Memory formation drives retrospective time perception

insights.claim: Retrospective time judgment ('this week flew by') depends almost entirely on how many distinct, novel memories were formed during a period; social-media and app usage generates high in-the-moment stimulation but leaves little behind in memory, producing a paradox where heavily-mediated time feels both fast in the moment and empty/compressed in retrospect.
insights.speaker: Mike Mariani
insights.so_what: Explains a core tension in consumer digital products: engagement metrics (time-on-app) may be inversely correlated with the kind of memorable experience that builds long-term brand/platform loyalty or life satisfaction, a risk for social-media platforms facing 'digital wellbeing' backlash.
insights.quote: When you get to the end of the day, you look back and there’s no meaningful content there. It’s just the same blur, the same stuff, and there’s nothing distinctive about it.
insights.locator: A Theory Of Relativity section, Luke Jones quote

insights.claim: The TIMED research consortium (multi-country European study spanning Germany, Spain, Switzerland, UK, three years, tens of thousands of participants) found that people who spend more time on devices and social media experience time passing more quickly, and links this to reduced 'novel, embodied, and enactive experiences' that would otherwise be encoded into autobiographical memory.
insights.speaker: Mike Mariani
insights.so_what: A large, multi-year empirical dataset directly linking device/social-media use to time-perception distortion and negative affect (guilt, shame, loss-of-control feelings) — a citable evidence base for digital-wellbeing regulation, product design ethics, or ESG-style 'social harm' assessments of platform companies.
insights.quote: Routine activities such as repeatedly checking apps or prolonged online engagement for professional purposes could reduce the frequency of novel, embodied, and enactive experiences.
insights.locator: Investigating The Time Warp section, TIMED paper quote

insights.claim: TIMED interview participants associated digital technology use with 'a loss of time, a desire to fill all time, a propensity to forget time' and this in turn produced feelings of guilt, shame, and lack of self-control.
insights.speaker: Mike Mariani
insights.so_what: Documents a measurable negative psychological externality of engagement-optimized apps, relevant to litigation/regulatory narratives (e.g., state AG suits against social platforms) framing addictive design as harmful.
insights.quote: Participants associated digital technology use with a loss of time, a desire to fill all time, a propensity to forget time and, as a result, a desire to gain greater control of time.

themes.theme: The pandemic as a discrete natural experiment

insights.claim: A 2023 Baylor University study using Gallup pandemic-era data found Americans experienced 'time disorientation' in multiple, sometimes contradictory directions during Covid — time speeding up, slowing down, and days blending together — while a 2022 'Time & Society' study of Uruguayan students found 80% felt time had sped up or slowed down, with similar findings replicated in Argentina and Iraq.
insights.speaker: Mike Mariani
insights.so_what: Establishes the pandemic as a globally-replicated natural experiment in time-perception distortion, useful baseline for any research or product testing framework studying attention/wellbeing 'shocks.'
insights.locator: A Theory Of Relativity section, Baylor/Time & Society studies

insights.claim: Time perception researcher Marc Wittmann argues the pandemic's lack of distinct day-to-day markers (no more 'Monday is skating day') caused 'Blursday' — a specific disorientation pattern where every day looked identical, contributing to time compression in memory.
insights.speaker: Marc Wittmann
entities: Institute for Frontier Areas in Psychology and Mental Health
insights.so_what: Offers a portable diagnostic concept ('Blursday') for identifying when routine-flattening (e.g., remote work, algorithmic scheduling) is degrading memory formation and wellbeing, applicable beyond the pandemic to any monotony-inducing work environment.
insights.quote: Every day was the same. Monday used to be the day you went skating, Tuesday was the day you spent with your friends. We used to have something associated with each day.
insights.locator: A Theory Of Relativity section, Wittmann 'Blursday' quote

insights.claim: The author argues that post-pandemic 'porousness' between work and home life — accelerated by Slack, Teams, and Zoom — has kept people in a chronically overstimulated, anxious state that has prevented time perception from ever reverting to its pre-Covid pace.
insights.speaker: Mike Mariani
insights.so_what: Frames workplace-communication-tool ubiquity as a structural, not transient, driver of sustained collective 'time is speeding up' sentiment — relevant to enterprise-software vendors and to employers evaluating always-on culture's cost to retention/wellbeing.
insights.locator: The Beauty Of Boredom section, discussion of Slack/Teams/Zoom

themes.theme: Boredom as a scarce, undervalued resource

insights.claim: TIMED lead investigator Ruth Ogden argues society has wrongly stigmatized 'doing nothing' as laziness, and that the responsibility for reducing time distortion should shift from individuals to platform designers, since 'the key metric for the success of digital technology is how long users are on it for.'
insights.speaker: Ruth Ogden
insights.so_what: A direct critique of engagement-time as the core KPI of digital platforms — supports the thesis that a shift toward 'time well spent' metrics (already floated by some platforms) could become a genuine regulatory or competitive differentiator.
insights.quote: Maybe it’s time that we shifted some of that onto the creators. The key metric for the success of digital technology is how long users are on it for, and how many people they can get on it for as long as possible. How do we flip that?
insights.locator: The Beauty Of Boredom section, Ruth Ogden quote

insights.claim: Calm, unstimulated mental states ('quiet longueurs') activate a specific brain network responsible for memory-making, meaning idle time is not wasted time but a precondition for forming the memories that give retrospective time its depth.
insights.speaker: James Hyman
insights.so_what: Provides a neuroscience-based rationale for 'digital detox' or boredom-permitting product/workplace features as genuinely improving perceived quality of life, not just a lifestyle fad.
insights.quote: It’s in those calm moments where we see a unique pattern of activity in the part of our brain responsible for helping to make our memories.
insights.locator: The Beauty Of Boredom section, James Hyman quote
